items.stem: Which of the following best describes "magnetic field"?
options: The region around a magnet where a magnetic material or another magnet experiences a force
A device in which an electromagnet repeatedly attracts a soft iron armature, breaking the circuit each time, so the hammer strikes a gong
The force on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field
A long coil of wire that produces a magnetic field similar to a bar magnet when a current flows
items.answer: The region around a magnet where a magnetic material or another magnet experiences a force
items.markingKey: A. "magnetic field" is the region around a magnet where a magnetic material or another magnet experiences a force.

items.stem: Distinguish between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet.
items.answer: A permanent magnet has its own magnetic field all the time; an induced magnet is a magnetic material that becomes magnetic only while it is in another magnetic field.
items.markingKey: A permanent magnet has its own magnetic field all the time; an induced magnet is a magnetic material that becomes magnetic only while it is in another magnetic field. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Elena writes: "The Earth’s geographic North Pole is a magnetic north pole." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It attracts the north pole of a compass, so it behaves as a magnetic south pole.
items.markingKey: It attracts the north pole of a compass, so it behaves as a magnetic south pole. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Omar is investigating how the distance between a magnet and a steel paper clip affects the force of attraction. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If the distance increases, then the force will decrease rapidly, because the magnetic field gets weaker further from the pole as field lines spread out.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If the distance increases, then the force will decrease rapidly, because the magnetic field gets weaker further from the pole as field lines spread out.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the distance between a magnet and a steel paper clip affects the force of attraction. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): strong magnets can trap fingers; keep away from phones and bank cards. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. strong magnets can trap fingers; keep away from phones and bank cards); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "soft magnetic material".
items.answer: A material such as iron that is easily magnetised and loses its magnetism easily
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a material such as iron that is easily magnetised and loses its magnetism easily. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between steel and soft iron.
items.answer: Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily (used in electromagnets and transformers); steel is harder to magnetise but keeps its magnetism (used for permanent magnets).
items.markingKey: Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily (used in electromagnets and transformers); steel is harder to magnetise but keeps its magnetism (used for permanent magnets). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Magnetic field lines can cross each other." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Field lines never cross; at any point the field has only one direction.
items.markingKey: Field lines never cross; at any point the field has only one direction. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to the Earth’s magnetic field and the aurora, explain how it illustrates magnetic fields exerting forces.
items.answer: Charged particles from the Sun are guided by the Earth’s magnetic field towards the poles, producing the aurora borealis seen in Norway, Iceland and Canada. The field deflects charged particles, protecting the surface from much of the solar wind and concentrating particles near the poles.
items.markingKey: Context (Charged particles from the Sun are guided by the Earth’s magnetic field towards the poles, producing the aurora borealis seen in Norway, Iceland and Canada.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The field deflects charged particles, protecting the surface from much of the solar wind and concentrating particles near the poles. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to magnetic fields exerting forces.

items.stem: Omar writes: "Magnetic field lines can cross each other." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Field lines never cross; at any point the field has only one direction.
items.markingKey: Field lines never cross; at any point the field has only one direction. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Describe how you would use a plotting compass to draw the magnetic field pattern around a bar magnet, and explain how the pattern changes when two bar magnets are placed with (a) opposite poles and (b) like poles facing each other.
items.answer: Place the magnet on paper; put the compass near the N pole, mark the end of the needle, move the compass so its tail is at the mark, repeat to the S pole; draw a smooth line with arrows N→S; repeat from different starting points. (a) Lines go straight across the gap from N to S – strong, uniform field (attraction). (b) Lines push apart and a neutral point with no field forms midway (repulsion).
items.markingKey: Place the magnet on paper; put the compass near the N pole, mark the end of the needle, move the compass so its tail is at the mark, repeat to the S pole; draw a smooth line with arrows N→S; repeat from different starting points. (a) Lines go straight across the gap from N to S – strong, uniform field (attraction). (b) Lines push apart and a neutral point with no field forms midway (repulsion).

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "soft iron core".
items.answer: A core of easily magnetised iron placed inside a coil to make its magnetic field much stronger
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a core of easily magnetised iron placed inside a coil to make its magnetic field much stronger. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why the field inside a long solenoid is strong and uniform.
items.answer: The fields from each turn add together inside the coil, producing parallel, closely spaced field lines.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The fields from each turn add together inside the coil, producing parallel, closely spaced field lines. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a permanent magnet and an electromagnet.
items.answer: An electromagnet works only while current flows and its strength can be changed; a permanent magnet always has its field and its strength is fixed.
items.markingKey: An electromagnet works only while current flows and its strength can be changed; a permanent magnet always has its field and its strength is fixed. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe MRI scanners in hospitals and explain what it reveals about the strength of electromagnets.
items.answer: Superconducting electromagnets cooled with liquid helium produce fields of 1.5-3 T, tens of thousands of times stronger than the Earth’s field. Very large currents in many turns of superconducting wire produce an extremely strong, uniform field inside the solenoid.
items.markingKey: Context (Superconducting electromagnets cooled with liquid helium produce fields of 1.5-3 T, tens of thousands of times stronger than the Earth’s field.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Very large currents in many turns of superconducting wire produce an extremely strong, uniform field inside the solenoid. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the strength of electromagnets.

items.stem:
Lukas predicts the outcome of an investigation into how the number of turns on an electromagnet affects its strength.
(a) Formulate a hypothesis that includes a scientific explanation. [2]
(b) Identify the independent and dependent variables. [2]
(c) State two variables that must be controlled. [1]
(d) Sketch the shape of the graph you would expect if the hypothesis is correct and explain how it would support the hypothesis. [1]
items.answer: (a) If the number of turns increases, then the electromagnet will pick up more clips, because each turn adds to the magnetic field, making it stronger. (b) IV: number of turns of wire (10, 20, 30, 40, 50); DV: strength – number of identical steel paper clips picked up (or force on a newton meter / reading on a magnetometer). (c) current (set with a variable resistor and checked on an ammeter); time the current flows. (d) A graph of the DV against the IV showing the predicted trend; if the data follow this trend within the spread of repeats, the hypothesis is supported.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 testable prediction; 1 scientific reasoning: If the number of turns increases, then the electromagnet will pick up more clips, because each turn adds to the magnetic field, making it stronger. (b) 1 IV: number of turns of wire (10, 20, 30, 40, 50); 1 DV: strength – number of identical steel paper clips picked up (or force on a newton meter / reading on a magnetometer). (c) 1 any two of current (set with a variable resistor and checked on an ammeter) (a larger current makes a stronger field); the same iron nail core (core material affects strength); type of paper clip (mass and steel type); time the current flows (the wire heats up and resistance changes). (d) 1 graph shape consistent with the hypothesis, linked to support.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Maglev trains are a better investment than conventional high-speed rail."
items.answer: Maglev is technically impressive, but conventional high-speed rail is usually more cost-effective unless very high speed on a dedicated route is essential.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: higher speeds, low friction, less wear and noise; very smooth ride. Arguments against: much higher construction cost; incompatible with existing rail networks; high energy use at top speed. Supported judgement: Maglev is technically impressive, but conventional high-speed rail is usually more cost-effective unless very high speed on a dedicated route is essential.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "electromagnet"?
options: A magnet that produces its own magnetic field all the time
A coil of wire, usually wrapped around a soft iron core, that becomes a magnet when a current flows
An electromagnetic switch in which a small current in one circuit operates an electromagnet that switches on a larger current in a second circuit
A device in which an electromagnet repeatedly attracts a soft iron armature, breaking the circuit each time, so the hammer strikes a gong
items.answer: A coil of wire, usually wrapped around a soft iron core, that becomes a magnet when a current flows
items.markingKey: B. "electromagnet" is a coil of wire, usually wrapped around a soft iron core, that becomes a magnet when a current flows.

items.stem: Briefly explain why adding a soft iron core makes a solenoid’s field much stronger.
items.answer: The iron becomes magnetised (induced magnetism) by the solenoid’s field, adding its own strong field to that of the coil.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The iron becomes magnetised (induced magnetism) by the solenoid’s field, adding its own strong field to that of the coil. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "An electromagnet works because the current flows through the iron core." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The current flows only in the coil; the core is magnetised by the coil’s field.
items.markingKey: The current flows only in the coil; the core is magnetised by the coil’s field. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using the Shanghai maglev train as an example, explain uses of electromagnets.
items.answer: Electromagnets on the train and track lift it above the guideway and propel it at up to 431 km/h. Switching currents in the electromagnets controls attraction and repulsion, removing wheel friction.
items.markingKey: Context (Electromagnets on the train and track lift it above the guideway and propel it at up to 431 km/h.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A split-ring in a DC motor that reverses the current in the coil every half turn so it keeps rotating in the same direction"?
options: motor effect
soft iron core
commutator
armature
items.answer: commutator
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of commutator.

items.stem: A student claims that a DC motor needs a commutator because the current would otherwise stop. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Without a commutator the current would keep flowing but the coil would only rock back and forth, because the forces would reverse their turning effect every half turn.
items.markingKey: Without a commutator the current would keep flowing but the coil would only rock back and forth, because the forces would reverse their turning effect every half turn. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that in Fleming’s left-hand rule, the thumb shows the direction of the current. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The thumb shows motion (force); the second finger shows current and the first finger shows field.
items.markingKey: The thumb shows motion (force); the second finger shows current and the first finger shows field. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Michael Faraday’s first motor (1821) shows the motor effect.
items.answer: A wire carrying current hung into a dish of mercury with a magnet in the middle; the wire rotated continuously around the magnet. The magnetic field of the current interacted with the magnet’s field, giving a continuous force on the wire.
items.markingKey: Context (A wire carrying current hung into a dish of mercury with a magnet in the middle; the wire rotated continuously around the magnet.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The magnetic field of the current interacted with the magnet’s field, giving a continuous force on the wire. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the motor effect.

items.stem: A straight wire carries current towards the west, in a magnetic field pointing upwards. Use Fleming’s left-hand rule to state the direction of the force on the wire.
items.answer: north
items.markingKey: 1 first finger along the field (up), second finger along the current (west); 1 thumb gives force: north.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that electric motors should replace internal combustion engines in all public buses within ten years.
items.answer: Rapid electrification is achievable in many cities with investment, as Shenzhen shows, but timelines depend on funding and grid capacity.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: zero tailpipe emissions improve urban air quality (e.g. Shenzhen’s fully electric fleet); lower running and maintenance costs. Arguments against: high purchase cost and charging infrastructure; battery supply chains and range in cold climates; electricity may come from fossil fuels. Supported judgement: Rapid electrification is achievable in many cities with investment, as Shenzhen shows, but timelines depend on funding and grid capacity.

items.stem: When is the force on a wire in a magnetic field zero?
options: When the wire is parallel to the field lines
When the magnet is strong
When the wire is at 90° to the field
When the current is large
items.answer: When the wire is parallel to the field lines
items.markingKey: A. Force is greatest at 90° and zero when parallel.

items.stem: Distinguish between electromagnetic induction and the motor effect.
items.answer: The motor effect: current + magnetic field → force/motion (motors, loudspeakers); induction: motion + magnetic field → induced voltage/current (generators, microphones).
items.markingKey: The motor effect: current + magnetic field → force/motion (motors, loudspeakers); induction: motion + magnetic field → induced voltage/current (generators, microphones). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

Ana placed a magnet on a top-pan balance with a fixed copper rod between its poles and recorded the force on the rod for different currents.

1.5 | 18.2 | 18.5 | 19.3

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The force increases in direct proportion to the current. F = BIL: with the field strength and length in the field constant, the force is proportional to the current (motor effect).

items.stem: Describe how a simple DC motor works, referring to the coil, magnets, split-ring commutator and brushes. Explain why the motor would only rock back and forth without the commutator, and state two ways to reverse the direction of rotation.
items.answer: Current flows through the coil via brushes and commutator; the motor effect produces upward force on one side and downward force on the other, creating a turning effect. Every half turn the commutator reverses the current so forces keep turning the coil the same way. Without it, after half a turn the forces would turn it back, so it would oscillate. Reverse the current or reverse the magnetic field (swap the magnets).
items.markingKey: Current flows through the coil via brushes and commutator; the motor effect produces upward force on one side and downward force on the other, creating a turning effect. Reverse the current or reverse the magnetic field (swap the magnets).

The region around a magnet where a magnetic material or another magnet experiences a force

items.stem: Explain how a loudspeaker produces sound.
items.answer: An alternating current flows in a coil in the field of a permanent magnet; the motor effect gives a force that reverses with the current, so the coil and attached cone vibrate, producing pressure waves in the air.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: An alternating current flows in a coil in the field of a permanent magnet; the motor effect gives a force that reverses with the current, so the coil and attached cone vibrate, producing pressure waves in the air. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Isabel writes: "In a relay the large current flows through the electromagnet coil." Explain why this is inaccurate.

items.markingKey: Only the small control current flows through the coil; the large current flows in the separate switched circuit. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that a louder sound from a loudspeaker means the current has a higher frequency. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Louder means a larger amplitude of current (bigger vibrations); higher frequency gives higher pitch.

items.stem: Briefly describe railway signalling interlocks and explain what it reveals about relays as switches.
items.answer: For decades, banks of relays ensured that conflicting signals could not show green at the same time. Small control currents operated relays that safely switched signal lamps and points, and wiring between relays prevented dangerous combinations.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that electromagnetic relays should be replaced by electronic (solid-state) switches in all devices.
items.answer: Solid-state switches are better for many low-power and fast uses, but relays remain useful where isolation and high currents matter.

Arguments against: relays give complete electrical isolation between circuits; relays handle surges and high currents well and are cheap; easy to see and test. items.answer: Only the small control current flows through the coil; the large current flows in the separate switched circuit.
items.markingKey: Only the small control current flows through the coil; the large current flows in the separate switched circuit. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Zara writes: "An electromagnet works because the current flows through the iron core." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The current flows only in the coil; the core is magnetised by the coil’s field.
items.markingKey: The current flows only in the coil; the core is magnetised by the coil’s field. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "The Earth’s geographic North Pole is a magnetic north pole." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It attracts the north pole of a compass, so it behaves as a magnetic south pole.
items.markingKey: It attracts the north pole of a compass, so it behaves as a magnetic south pole. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the motor effect and electromagnetic induction.
items.answer: The motor effect: current + magnetic field → force/motion (motors, loudspeakers); induction: motion + magnetic field → induced voltage/current (generators, microphones).
items.markingKey: The motor effect: current + magnetic field → force/motion (motors, loudspeakers); induction: motion + magnetic field → induced voltage/current (generators, microphones). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how a relay works.
items.answer: A small current flows through the relay coil, making it an electromagnet; this attracts an iron armature, which closes contacts in a second circuit, switching on a large current.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A small current flows through the relay coil, making it an electromagnet; this attracts an iron armature, which closes contacts in a second circuit, switching on a large current. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between an electromagnet and a solenoid.
items.answer: A solenoid is a coil of wire that produces a magnetic field when current flows; an electromagnet is usually a solenoid with a soft iron core, making the field much stronger.
items.markingKey: A solenoid is a coil of wire that produces a magnetic field when current flows; an electromagnet is usually a solenoid with a soft iron core, making the field much stronger. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to magnetic separation of scrap metal in recycling plants, explain how it illustrates magnetic and non-magnetic materials.
items.answer: Large magnets lift steel and iron cans from mixed waste, leaving aluminium cans behind. Steel is magnetic and is attracted to the magnet; aluminium is not.
items.markingKey: Context (Large magnets lift steel and iron cans from mixed waste, leaving aluminium cans behind.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Briefly describe electric bicycles in cities such as Amsterdam and Shenzhen and explain what it reveals about the motor effect.
items.answer: Hub motors use the motor effect: current in coils inside a ring of permanent magnets produces a force that turns the wheel. Current-carrying coils in a magnetic field experience forces that create a turning effect.
items.markingKey: Context (Hub motors use the motor effect: current in coils inside a ring of permanent magnets produces a force that turns the wheel.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Outline one way in which MRI scanners in hospitals shows the strength of electromagnets.
items.answer: Superconducting electromagnets cooled with liquid helium produce fields of 1.5-3 T, tens of thousands of times stronger than the Earth’s field. Very large currents in many turns of superconducting wire produce an extremely strong, uniform field inside the solenoid.

items.stem: Chloé plans to investigate how the current through a wire affects the force on it in a magnetic field (the motor effect), measured with a top-pan balance. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: length of wire in the field; the same pair of magnets and spacing; angle of wire to field (90°); zeroing the balance

items.stem: Briefly describe hearing-aid and headphone drivers and explain what it reveals about the loudspeaker principle.
items.answer: Tiny moving-coil drivers convert audio signals into sound close to the ear. A varying current in a small coil in a magnetic field vibrates a diaphragm at the frequency of the signal.
items.markingKey: Context (Tiny moving-coil drivers convert audio signals into sound close to the ear.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Describe how the right-hand grip rule is used to find the poles of a solenoid, and explain three ways to increase the strength of an electromagnet. Suggest why there is a limit to how much the strength can be increased by raising the current.
items.answer: Curl the fingers of the right hand in the direction of conventional current around the coil; the thumb points to the north pole. Stronger: more turns, larger current, soft iron core (also shorter/closer turns). Limit: wires heat up (I²R), insulation can melt, and the iron core saturates so extra current adds little.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that magnetic levitation and strong magnets in consumer products (e.g. magnetic toys) pose too great a risk to children.
items.answer: Strong small magnets in toys need strict regulation, but magnets in general are safe and beneficial.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: swallowed powerful magnets can attract through the intestine walls, causing serious injury; magnets can damage pacemakers and cards. Arguments against: magnets are very useful and widely safe when used properly; labelling and size rules reduce risk. Supported judgement: Strong small magnets in toys need strict regulation, but magnets in general are safe and beneficial. items.stem: To what extent is it true that replacing petrol engines with electric motors in all vehicles would solve urban pollution?
items.answer: Electric motors greatly reduce urban air pollution but do not eliminate it; the overall benefit depends on clean electricity and battery recycling.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: no exhaust emissions in cities, quieter streets; motors are about 90% efficient. Arguments against: brake and tyre particles still pollute; electricity may be generated from fossil fuels elsewhere; battery production has environmental costs. Supported judgement: Electric motors greatly reduce urban air pollution but do not eliminate it; the overall benefit depends on clean electricity and battery recycling. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: A greenhouse fan (230 V, 5 A) must switch on automatically when a 6 V temperature-sensing circuit detects high temperature. Explain, with a labelled circuit description, how a relay allows this, and give two safety advantages of using a relay.
items.answer: The sensing circuit (thermistor, 6 V) switches current through the relay coil; the coil becomes an electromagnet, attracts the armature and closes contacts in the separate 230 V fan circuit. Advantages: the low-voltage circuit is electrically isolated from mains; small, safe currents in the control wires; the user never touches the mains circuit.
items.markingKey: The sensing circuit (thermistor, 6 V) switches current through the relay coil; the coil becomes an electromagnet, attracts the armature and closes contacts in the separate 230 V fan circuit. items.stem: What is the purpose of the split-ring commutator?
items.answer: To reverse the current in the coil every half turn
items.markingKey: To reverse the current in the coil every half turn. This keeps the turning effect in one direction.

items.stem: Distinguish between an ordinary switch and a relay.
items.answer: An ordinary switch is operated by hand and carries the full current; a relay is operated by a small current in its coil and switches a separate, larger current.

items.stem: "Using a copper core would make an electromagnet stronger because copper is a good conductor." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Copper is not magnetic, so it does not increase the field; soft iron is used.

items.stem: Explain the difference between steel and soft iron.
items.answer: Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily (used in electromagnets and transformers); steel is harder to magnetise but keeps its magnetism (used for permanent magnets).
items.markingKey: Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily (used in electromagnets and transformers); steel is harder to magnetise but keeps its magnetism (used for permanent magnets). items.stem: Explain how a simple DC motor keeps turning in the same direction.
items.answer: Forces on opposite sides of the coil act in opposite directions, creating a turning effect; the split-ring commutator reverses the current every half turn, so the forces keep turning the coil the same way.

items.stem: Explain why an electromagnet is more useful than a permanent magnet in a scrapyard crane.
items.answer: The electromagnet can be switched off, so the crane can release the scrap metal where needed; its strength can also be adjusted by changing the current.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Earth’s magnetic field and the aurora and explain what it reveals about magnetic fields exerting forces.
items.answer: Charged particles from the Sun are guided by the Earth’s magnetic field towards the poles, producing the aurora borealis seen in Norway, Iceland and Canada. The field deflects charged particles, protecting the surface from much of the solar wind and concentrating particles near the poles.

Alessia is investigating how the frequency of the signal sent to a loudspeaker affects the loudness of the sound produced at a fixed input voltage. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.

items.answer: For decades, banks of relays ensured that conflicting signals could not show green at the same time. Small control currents operated relays that safely switched signal lamps and points, and wiring between relays prevented dangerous combinations.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the number of turns on an electromagnet affects its strength. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Wind 10 turns of insulated wire around an iron nail; connect to a low-voltage supply, ammeter and variable resistor; set 1.0 A; dip into a tray of clips and lift; count clips; switch off between trials; repeat 3 times; repeat with 20-50 turns.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the current through a wire affects the force on it in a magnetic field (the motor effect), measured with a top-pan balance. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Place a U-shaped magnet on a top-pan balance and zero it; clamp a stiff copper rod horizontally between the poles, not touching; pass 0.5, 1.0 … 3.0 A through the rod; record the change in reading; force = Δm × 9.8 (Δm in kg); repeat 3 times; plot force against current.

items.stem: "Electromagnetic relays should be replaced by electronic (solid-state) switches in all devices." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Solid-state switches are better for many low-power and fast uses, but relays remain useful where isolation and high currents matter.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: no moving parts so no wear or sparking; faster switching and silent; smaller. Arguments against: relays give complete electrical isolation between circuits; relays handle surges and high currents well and are cheap; easy to see and test. Supported judgement: Solid-state switches are better for many low-power and fast uses, but relays remain useful where isolation and high currents matter.
